title: Hinsdale County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Hinsdale County the median well depth is 86 ft and the median yield is 15 gpm. Learn what that means for drilling costs, water level and buying land.
h1: Water wells in Hinsdale County, Colorado
intro_html:
Hinsdale County is classic high-country fractured bedrock. More than half of the wells on record are under 100 feet, but there are also a few that run hundreds of feet deep. Before you buy land or plan a build, it helps to know what the local numbers say about depth, yield, water levels, and costs.

These figures come from 1,257 well permits spread around the county, including the Lake City area and the more remote backroads. They give a pretty clear picture of what to expect from a new domestic well here.

sections.heading: How deep Hinsdale County wells really are
sections.html:
Across Hinsdale County, the median well depth is 86 feet, with the middle half running from 42 to 200 feet. That tells you a “typical” domestic well here is not especially deep by mountain standards, but there is wide variation. About 53% of wells are under 100 feet, while 29% are between 100 and 300 feet, and 15% run 300 to 600 feet. Around 2% are 600 feet or deeper, and the deepest well on record reaches 1,780 feet.

For bidding, a driller is going to look at nearby wells and probably price you assuming something in that 42–200 foot band, but with fractured granite and gneiss, nobody can promise a final depth. The mix of shallow and very deep holes here is exactly what you expect in hard-rock mountains.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you can expect
sections.html:
Out of the Hinsdale wells that report production, the median yield is 15.0 gpm, with the middle half between 7.0 and 15.0 gpm. That’s strong for household and stock use. More than half of tested wells, 54%, pump 15+ gpm, while 32% land in the 5–15 gpm range. Only 12% come in between 1 and 5 gpm, and about 2% report under 1 gpm.

For an exempt domestic well on a single home, even 1–2 gpm can work with storage, and 7–15 gpm is very comfortable. The fractured-bedrock aquifer is unpredictable from hole to hole, but overall this county’s yield numbers are favorable compared with a lot of Colorado mountain areas.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they’re doing over time
sections.html:
Static water levels are the depth from ground surface down to the water in the well. In Hinsdale County, the overall median static level is 40 feet, with the middle half between 19 and 75 feet. That means many pumps are set only a modest distance below grade, which helps on installation and power costs.

Looking at measurements by decade, the median depth to water in the 2010s was 88 feet, while in the 2020s it’s 30 feet. Shallower numbers mean the water is closer to the surface, so the limited data we have suggest water levels have been stable to improving in recent years rather than dropping.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and permit patterns
sections.html:
Hinsdale County has 1,257 well permits on record, with 838 listed as constructed and 816 reporting a total depth. Domestic and household use dominates at 78% of permits, with smaller shares for stock, irrigation, and monitoring. Most wells are completed in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers; a handful tap the Unconfined San Luis Valley and local alluvium.

Drilling picked up in the 1970s and 1980s, with 138 permits in the 1970s and 230 in the 1980s, then 256 in the 1990s. The pace tapered to 194 in the 2000s, 111 in the 2010s, and 68 so far in the 2020s, with the newest permit in 2025. The most active drillers on record are Bob Williams Drilling Co., Irrigation Engineering & Supp., and Valley Pump Company.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Hinsdale County
sections.html:
Here the subsurface is fractured mountain bedrock, mainly granite and gneiss. Typical drilling rates run about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s median depth of 86 feet, that puts the bare hole in the ballpark of $5,600–$8,600.

When you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, wiring, and tie-in to the house, a finished domestic well at that depth usually comes out around $11,600–$20,600. If your well ends up deeper than the median—say out in that 200–300 foot range you see in the local data—cost scales almost linearly with depth, so it’s smart to budget with a safety margin.

sections.heading: Risks to check: low yield, contamination, and siting
sections.html:
Only a small share of Hinsdale wells report under 1 gpm, about 2%, and 12% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. That’s your main performance risk: you probably get water, but you might need storage if you land in the low-yield tail. On the contamination side, the county has 4 mapped PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 805 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles.

Before drilling or buying, look up nearby wells, check mapped mine and cleanup sites, and plan solid setbacks between well, septic, and any creeks or drainages. In fractured bedrock, grout and proper surface sealing are your best protection from shallow surface impacts.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Hinsdale County well lot
sections.html:
When you’re evaluating a parcel in Hinsdale County or around Lake City, start by pulling nearby well permits. If most neighbors are 40–200 feet deep with 7–15 gpm yields, that’s encouraging, but remember a few holes go far deeper and a handful are low-yield. Plan for the median depth of 86 feet, but budget as if you might need more.

Confirm you can get a domestic well permit for the use you want, and understand the standard 35 gpm exempt-well pumping cap for household and limited outside use. On raw land, also verify there’s good access for a rig, room for a septic system, and logical house and driveway locations before you close.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Hinsdale County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Hinsdale County, the median well depth is 86 feet, with the middle half of wells between 42 and 200 feet deep. About 53% are under 100 feet, another 29% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 15% are 300 to 600 feet. Only about 2% are deeper than 600 feet, but the single deepest well on record reaches 1,780 feet.

faq.q: How much water do Hinsdale County wells produce?
faq.a: Reported production is generally solid. The median yield is 15.0 gpm, and the middle half of wells fall in the 7.0–15.0 gpm range. More than half, 54%, are 15+ gpm, and 32% produce 5–15 gpm. Only 12% of wells report 1–5 gpm and about 2% are under 1 gpm, where you’d likely plan on a storage tank to make the well practical for a home.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Hinsdale County, CO?
faq.a: In Hinsdale’s fractured granite and gneiss, typical drilling runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s median 86-foot depth, that means roughly $5,600–$8,600 for the drilled hole. By the time you add pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a complete domestic system at that depth usually totals around $11,600–$20,600, with deeper wells scaling up from there.

faq.q: Are well water levels dropping in Hinsdale County?
faq.a: Available static water level data do not show a clear countywide decline. Overall, the median depth to water is 40 feet, with a middle half between 19 and 75 feet. By decade, the median was 88 feet in the 2010s and 30 feet in the 2020s. Those more recent measurements are shallower, which suggests water has been stable to improving in the limited records we have.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Hinsdale County, Colorado?
faq.a: Most wells tap fractured bedrock aquifers, which are generally clean, but the county also has 4 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, about 805 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles. Because of that, it’s wise to test any existing well for bacteria and metals at a minimum, and consider broader panels if you’re near old mining or cleanup areas.
